book_context: The plot runs as a chain of small coincidences. Tommy's overheard name leads to Whittington, the advertisement brings Carter and Julius, and the survivor list yields Rita. Each lead opens the next, and Mr. Brown repeatedly strikes just ahead of them. Chapters IV–VII set up the governing premises: the Danvers/Lusitania backstory, the draft treaty, and the Brown method. That method means a nondescript, overlooked figure behind someone else, a common name, and the unanswerable 'one of us'. These chapters also introduce Julius, with his genealogy and the single photograph, and tie Rita to the name Marguerite. Later revelations depend on all of this: the identity of Mr. Brown, the false Jane at Manchester, the photograph in Julius's drawer, Annette's 'Marguerite' cry, and the 29th. Early chapters must plant these premises neutrally, without foreshadowing the solution.

essential: The narrator draws a veil: Inspector Brown was unknown to Scotland Yard, the photograph is lost for good, and Brown has triumphed again.
The set-back brings them close to Julius. They tell him everything; his remark on 'moss-grown' English girls; the move to the Ritz justified as keeping in touch with Jane's only relation.
Breakfast banter: Tuppence demands action, while Tommy applauds, cites his 'union' and keeps reading the Daily Mail.
Clue one: Whittington, with Tommy's thousand-to-one objection, Tuppence's coincidence law, and the flag-tray idea punctured by meals.

Clue two: 'Rita'. Tuppence reasons that Danvers was shadowed, probably by a good-looking woman, who must have survived, since otherwise the gang could not know Jane had the papers. Tuppence admits it is 'only a chance'.
Carter sent the survivor list in reply to her questions, but most entries give only Mrs. or Miss, which complicates things. She lists the London addresses.
Tommy's Voting Register ruse at The Laurels: Mrs. Edgar Keith is Eleanor Jane; the servant's 'about the gas' line; Tommy's male smugness, which Tuppence concedes.
Lunch summary of the blanks, with Sadie's suffrage lecture. Mrs. Vandemeyer is next; Tuppence is discouraged and Tommy cheers her.
The banter about Brown having not yet 'done us to death' and Tommy's 'moles in the dark'. Its irony must remain.
At South Audley Mansions: 'Margaret', corrected to 'g u e'; Tommy's bold 'Rita Vandemeyer'; confirmation that Marguerite is her name.
They rejoice. Tuppence pulls Tommy into the shadow beside the lift, two men pass, and she tells him to follow because the bigger one is Whittington.

voice_profile: Light, brisk comic-thriller narration. The narrator is close to Tommy and Tuppence and mildly ironic about them, with mock-formal phrasing such as "Mr. Beresford obliged" and "Nobody did, which was the great thing." Most of the effect comes through dialogue. The two leads trade slangy banter ("old thing", "old bean", "Don't be a wretch") and deflate each other's vanity. They parody detective fiction and formal speech: plans of campaign, "Proceed, O Sherlock!", "a literary flavour". Tuppence frankly loves money; Tommy is slow, practical and deadpan. Mr. Carter speaks in a tired, reflective monotone of hedged exposition. Julius uses American idiom ("Put me wise", "Sure thing", "I guess") and gets things done by forceful, moneyed impatience. Menace arrives suddenly in a short closing line after comedy. The text uses double hyphens for breaks and interruptions, four-hyphen trailing-offs, ellipses, and underscore emphasis.
